prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and its experimental discovery in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I opened with B012 because the topological-insulator story is, for me, the cleanest example of a prediction followed by an experiment that nature could have refused: Kane and Mele proposed the Z2 quantum spin Hall state in 2005, and Molenkamp's group observed edge-channel transport in HgTe quantum wells in 2007. That is the original experiment, with a result that has since been reproduced in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and, through ARPES, in Bi-based three-dimensional materials. Having read the other seven ballots, I move to B042 as the vehicle. Five of eight members ranked it, three in their top three, and it credits Mele, whom my own B012 entry could not. Dropping Mele would leave the theory half of the prize with an arbitrary gap. Kane and Mele together plus Molenkamp is the most defensible mapping of who did what first that the supplied names allow. The field is mature, the interpretation is stable, and the work opens a door to protected states that people could not see before.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe prediction that told Molenkamp where to look, Zhang is deceased, and Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan carried the idea to three-dimensional materials, so any three names omit people with a real claim. Moving to B042 also gives up Xue's quantum anomalous Hall experiment, which I regard as a separate and genuine experimental discovery. The 2016 prize on topological phases of matter may also make colleagues feel the area has been honoured already, though that prize rewarded the topological concepts in phase transitions and the Thouless-Haldane integer quantum Hall lineage, not band topology in time-reversal-invariant insulators.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked B042 second, values the link to band-structure calculations and ARPES, and warns that the overlap with B012 forces the committee to choose one framing and that BHZ, Fu-Moore-Balents and Hasan complicate a three-person split.
responses.response: I agree that the two ballots are one field and must not be stacked. I now think B042 is the better framing because it credits Mele, and my own B012 depended on a QAH experiment that is a different discovery. I share your concern about BHZ and Hasan, but I do not think it defeats the case. The Kane-Mele proposal and the first HgTe observation are the traceable original steps, and the 3D work is a later extension that the citation need not cover. Where I differ from you is on ARPES. It confirms the 3D phase, but it is not the original experiment, and I would keep the citation tied to the quantum spin Hall observation.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked the Higgs observation (B006) first, arguing that the 2013 prize honoured only the theory and that the founding spokespersons are the natural names for the experiment.
responses.response: I ranked B006 second myself and agree that it is an original, verified, important experiment. My difficulty is the one you flag. The decisive discovery in 2012 rested on analysis teams, trigger and accelerator groups, and the spokespersons at the time of discovery were not Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee. Crediting detector conception honours real work, but it is closer to a prize for leadership than for the observation itself, and I want to be absolutely sure we have the people who did the original work. I would keep it as a fallback if the committee decides it can defend the credit, but I do not think it can lead until that is settled.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked the optical lattice clock (B037) first for its conceptual clarity and precision, with attribution to Katori and Ye, while noting that Hall and Hansch were honoured in 2005.
responses.response: I ranked B037 fourth, and I find the invention concrete and well verified: a new instrument at the 1e-18 level, reproduced across continents. I take the point that the credit is clean. My reservation is that the prospective benefits, namely redefining the second and relativistic geodesy, have not yet been delivered, and that the neighbouring 2005 and 2012 prizes cover the comb and ion-clock control. I would like AMO members to say whether the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct discovery or an evolutionary step, because that decides whether it is an original experiment or a better one. If you can make that case, B037 is a serious alternative to my preference.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED (B008) first and B042 third, noting that the BHZ omission is a real allocation problem and that the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits does not subsume cQED.
responses.response: I agree that BHZ is the weak point of B042 and I do not want to hide it. Where we may differ is on B008. Strong coupling in a chip is a clear original experiment, and I take your point on the 2025 prize, but I ranked it seventh because of the credit uncertainty around Girvin and the close adjacency to the committee's recent decision. I note your own declaration of proximity to that community and would treat it as a reason to hear the physics from you and weigh the ranking separately.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can accept a credit set that omits Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D topological-insulator experimenters.
Whether Xue's quantum anomalous Hall effect should be recognised as a separate achievement, which would require a different three-person split.
Whether the 2016 prize on topological phases lowers the appetite for another topology prize.
Whether the Higgs credit set could be settled in a way that satisfies the requirement that the people credited did the original work.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the B042, B012 or B037 candidates. My only note is that Goran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, which is relevant only to the circuit QED ballot he ranks first, not to my preferred configuration.
